common_name: Scallopini Squash (AAS-Winning Hybrid Bush Scallop Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil, thinning seedlings to give each compact bush adequate airflow to reduce powdery mildew risk.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil, thinning seedlings to give each compact bush adequate airflow to reduce powdery mildew risk. Introduced in the mid-1970s as an All-America Selections winner, this cross between zucchini and pattypan types yields small, dark-green scalloped fruit with a mild, nutty flavor and tender skin that needs no peeling. Harvest young at 3-4 inches across for the best texture, picking every day or two once plants begin producing heavily. Its compact, non-vining habit made it a popular choice for small-space and container vegetable gardens when it was introduced.

common_name: Cinnamon Girl Squash (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Butternut Hybrid)

planting.note: Sow directly outdoors once soil has warmed thoroughly, allowing semi-compact vines room to spread, and water consistently until fruit sets to support even sizing.

directions: Sow directly outdoors once soil has warmed thoroughly, allowing semi-compact vines room to spread, and water consistently until fruit sets to support even sizing. Named an All-America Selections winner in 2018, this hybrid butternut produces uniform, single-serving fruit around a pound each with deep tan skin and dense, sweet, richly colored flesh well suited to roasting whole. Bred for strong disease tolerance and heavy yields of personal-portion squash, it fits neatly into small households and market growers wanting consistent, easy-to-handle fruit. Cure harvested squash in a warm spot for a week or two to improve storage life and sweetness.

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger has passed, spacing plants for their semi-bush habit, and maintain even moisture as small acorn-shaped fruit begin to form.

directions: Direct sow after frost danger has passed, spacing plants for their semi-bush habit, and maintain even moisture as small acorn-shaped fruit begin to form and ripen to deep orange. Recognized as an All-America Selections winner in 2017, this hybrid was bred for markedly sweeter, less fibrous flesh than typical acorn squash along with strong resistance to powdery mildew that keeps foliage productive later into the season. Its semi-compact vines produce a heavy, uniform set of small fruit ideal for roasting or stuffing whole. Harvest once rinds are fully colored and hardened, then cure briefly before storing in a cool, dry space.

common_name: Ponca Baby Butternut Squash (AAS-Winning Mini Butternut)

planting.note: Sow seeds directly in warm soil after the last frost, spacing to allow moderate vine spread, and keep soil evenly moist to support a heavy set of small fruit.

directions: Sow seeds directly in warm soil after the last frost, spacing to allow moderate vine spread, and keep soil evenly moist to support a heavy set of small fruit. Developed by breeders at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and named an All-America Selections winner in 2021, this butternut produces compact, single-serving fruit under a pound with tan skin and dense, nutty-sweet orange flesh, bred with organic and small-farm production in mind. Its shorter vines and high fruit count per plant make it productive even in modest garden spaces. Allow fruit to fully harden on the vine before harvest, then cure for improved storage and flavor.

common_name: Berrettina Piacentina Squash (Italian Heirloom Turban Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil once frost has passed, giving sprawling vines ample room, and water deeply during fruit development to build dense flesh.

directions: Direct sow into warm soil once frost has passed, giving sprawling vines ample room, and water deeply during fruit development to build the dense flesh this variety is known for. Named for its distinctive tan, beret-like elongated turban shape, this traditional squash from the Piacenza province of Emilia-Romagna has long been grown for the region's celebrated tortelli di zucca, a pumpkin-filled pasta requiring dry, intensely sweet flesh. Its knobby, ridged rind and rich orange interior set it apart from rounder turban types, and it stores well through winter when cured properly. Regional seed houses in northern Italy have kept the variety in circulation for home and market gardeners alike.

common_name: Gold Nugget Squash (AAS-Winning Compact Bush Buttercup-Type Squash)

planting.note: Sow directly in warm soil after the last frost, spacing plants closely since this variety's bush habit needs far less room than sprawling buttercup types.

directions: Sow directly in warm soil after the last frost, spacing plants closely since this variety's bush habit needs far less room than sprawling buttercup types. Bred at North Dakota State University for the region's short, cool growing season and named an All-America Selections winner in 1966, it produces small, round, deep-orange fruit with sweet, fine-grained flesh similar to buttercup squash but ready weeks earlier. Its compact, non-vining plants make it a practical choice for northern gardens and small plots where space and season length are limited. Harvest once the rind resists thumbnail pressure, then cure briefly to concentrate sugars before storage.
